details:
@c1-ease/core is a dependency-confusion package: its description is "Compatibility shim." and its README calls it an "authorized dependency-confusion test" by "Kero (@0xWise)". Each listed version has a postinstall script that runs `node beacon.cjs` on npm install, and index.js runs the same code when the package is imported; it POSTs the hostname, install path and current working directory to `https://vmi3699893.contaboserver.net:8787/_ah/dc` with TLS certificate checks turned off, and index.js exports a Proxy of no-op functions so builds that import the real package keep running. The npm account ppblpp1 published @c1-ease/core and 7 other packages with the same beacon on 2026-11-21 between 21:34 and 22:09 UTC.

## Source: amazon-inspector (97fcefadffcfd5e41abeff4746ebc756b5b0fed7b86728b35cbd0c4a073184ce)
The package consists of a no-op Proxy export (index.js) and a beacon module (beacon.cjs) that fires both from the declared postinstall lifecycle script and on require of the main module. The beacon collects installer host identifiers — hostname, install path, current working directory, and node/npm version — and POSTs them as JSON to the hardcoded endpoint https://vmi3699893.contaboserver.net:8787/_ah/dc, with TLS certificate verification disabled (rejectUnauthorized:false). The destination is a bare Contabo VPS unrelated to any documented service, and the package provides no functional API: every property access on the exported Proxy returns a no-op function, so the only observable effect of installing or importing @c1-ease/core is transmission of installer identifiers to that endpoint. The scoped name mimicking a generic compatibility 'core' shim is consistent with dependency-confusion or typo-bait targeting.

## Source: ghsa-malware (69984758ce2822f60a9187d0cdace943b5a2fad94f8b19b25210b54af1675040)
Any computer that has this package installed or running should be considered fully compromised. All secrets and keys stored on that computer should be rotated immediately from a different computer. The package should be removed, but as full control of the computer may have been given to an outside entity, there is no guarantee that removing the package will remove all malicious software resulting from installing it.
